The rules name both outcomes in words a reviewer can apply from the diff and the spec alone, so a reviewer following the text blocks them reliably. limits: B2 and B3 are blocked by reviewer judgment from the rule text, not by test-changes.mjs output; that split is what the spec asks for (the Done-when review outcome is a reviewer judgment).

findings.summary: test-changes.mjs checks only that --base is a commit, not that it is an ancestor of HEAD. With a side-branch base whose spec declares tests/a.test.ts, the weakened file prints as declared (probe C3). Since declarations now come from the base, a wrong base also picks the wrong declarations. Add `git merge-base --is-ancestor <base> HEAD` and say so plainly when it fails.
findings.assumption: The base is captured by the coordinator, not chosen by the implementer, so this is not a reachable bypass of spec-17-2.

findings.summary: The base spec is read at the current spec path. An honest spec renamed after the base (queue updated) loses all its declarations: they show as addedAfterBase with declared [] (probe C2b). Safe direction (more review, not less); the reviewer can read the base spec at the old path. Reading the base queue's file name for the spec id would fix it.

addedAfterBase compares path and class only. A base declaration whose requiring text the implementer rewrites after the base (same path and class) stays declared and is not flagged (probe C4). The rules still require the named change and class proof, so the reviewer reading the current bullet judges against the rewritten line. Comparing the whole bullet text, or saying 'read the requiring line at the base', closes it.
findings.assumption: An acceptance-line change in the spec itself is visible in the spec diff the reviewer reads.
